_what_this_is: The entry gate, answered BEFORE drafting. The threshold question is whether a well-informed non-expert would confidently believe something the primary sources do not support.

belief._note: What the reader already believes, stated as they would state it. If you cannot write this sentence, there is nothing to correct and no subject -- which is how the tobacco-analogy candidate died.
belief.statement: Inclusive education works. Getting children with disabilities into ordinary local schools, training teachers to include them, and providing things like glasses, hearing aids or ramps raises enrolment and learning. Inclusive mainstream schooling beats separate special schools, though the evidence from poorer countries is probably thinner than it should be.
belief.how_we_know_they_believe_it: The coverage that settled it. Named outlets, quoted headlines. Not 'it is widely assumed'.

what_the_sources_show._note: What the primary sources actually support, and which sources.

direction._note: CORRECTS, CONFIRMS or NARROWS. This field exists so the contrarianism guard can count. A publication whose answer is always CORRECTS is performing scepticism rather than assessing evidence, and is not to be trusted.

reader_with_a_decision: Education ministry planners and donor or NGO programme officers (e.g. at the World Bank, UNICEF, FCDO, USAID or disability-focused NGOs). They are deciding which interventions to fund or scale for children with disabilities. The options include teacher training for inclusion, assistive devices and screening, school accessibility works, cash transfers or fee waivers, community-based rehabilitation linked to schooling, and special or resource-unit provision.

public_record_check._note: NOT 'has anybody published this'. On any contested question, somebody has. The question is whether it has been carried WHERE THIS READER WOULD FIND IT. Run the counterexample hunter on the belief statement, not on the finding.
public_record_check.our_contribution: translation, extension, or correction of the prior art -- say which

kill_condition: Rigorous primary evaluations (randomised or credible quasi-experimental studies) in low- and middle-income countries consistently show that disability-targeted education programmes improve enrolment, attendance and learning for children with disabilities. The same studies also show a clear ranking of programme types that matches the common view (inclusive and teacher-training approaches outperform segregated provision), so there is nothing to correct or add.

kill_condition_tested._note: Filled in AFTER going to look, by whoever looked.

scope._note: What the answer will and will not cover, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened, so scope cannot be fitted to the findings afterwards. An omission ruled OUT_OF_SCOPE, and a headline conclusion declared out of scope, must name the question's words or one of these entries (fix 2, docs/whu-fix2-omission-rulings-design.md section 2.4).
scope.covers: Programmes and interventions in low- and middle-income countries that aim to improve educational access, participation, completion or learning for children and young people (roughly school and post-school ages) with disabilities. It covers whether such programmes show effects overall and how effects compare across programme types and disability types.

out.what: Effectiveness of inclusive or special education in high-income countries
out.why: The question is limited to low- and middle-income settings, where school systems, resources and evidence differ substantially.

out.what: How many children with disabilities are out of school, and the size of the schooling gap
out.why: That is a descriptive prevalence question, not a question about whether interventions work.

out.what: Health, rehabilitation or functional outcomes of disability programmes not measured through education
out.why: The question concerns educational outcomes. Health effects belong to a different evidence base.

out.what: General education reforms not targeted at, or not reporting results for, children with disabilities
out.why: Effects on the average child cannot be assumed to apply to children with disabilities without disaggregated evidence.

out.what: Whether inclusive education is a legal or human-rights obligation (e.g. under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities)
out.why: That is a normative and legal question, separate from the empirical question of what works.

evidence_standard._note: What kinds of evidence the answer will weigh, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened (post-study fix 3, docs/whu-fix3-evidence-standard.md). 'measured': outcomes measured in trials, cohorts, evaluations. 'assessed': expert assessments -- systematic-review conclusions, IPCC confidence-rated statements, guideline recommendations. When they differ, the page states both and drops neither.
evidence_standard.measured: Effect estimates from primary impact evaluations, preferably randomised trials or credible quasi-experimental designs, in low- and middle-income countries. Relevant outcomes are enrolment, attendance, retention, completion, transition and learning or test scores for children with disabilities. Also counted are sample sizes, comparison conditions, disability types covered, and any cost data reported alongside effects.
evidence_standard.assessed: Certainty or confidence ratings that systematic reviews, evidence gap maps or expert panels assign to the body of evidence. Examples are GRADE ratings in Campbell or Cochrane-style reviews, and quality appraisals in 3ie or similar evidence maps. Also counted are reviewers' judgements about which programme types have adequate, limited or no evidence.
